To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the peripheral airway function of children with persistent asthma is impaired and that peripheral airway impairment is associated with asthma control.
The use of a single, simple, noninvasive, objective, quantitative measure of small airway function (oscillometry) can predict loss of asthma control and the need for additional treatment.

(i) the presence of peripheral airway obstruction in children with persistent asthma is associated with loss of asthma control; and (ii) the presence of airway hyperresponsiveness in children with persistent mild asthma is associated with a higher risk of loss of asthma control.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel methods and tools for the analysis of the structure and function of biological systems.
the use of a new technique, oscillometry, for the assessment of peripheral airways in asthmatic children.
the study of asthma control and its determinants in children and adolescents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is insufficient to determine the effect of a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol and high in fruits and vegetables on the incidence of asthma in children.
the use of inhaled corticosteroids in children with mild persistent asthma is beneficial.
the use of a single inhaler containing a LABA and a LAMA for the management of persistent asthma in children and adolescents aged 5 years and above is not recommended.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the oscillometry-derived measures of small airways function (SAP, SAP/FEV1, SAP/FRC) predict loss of asthma control, as measured by the Asthma Control Test (ACT), in children and adolescents with asthma.
the use of oscillometry as a tool to assess peripheral airway function can be used to identify asthma exacerbations before they occur, and can predict loss of asthma control.
the peripheral airways play a major role in asthma control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single test that will tell you whether you have asthma or not, and there is no one test that will tell your doctor what type of asthma you have.
there are some important differences in the effects of asthma and COPD in the peripheral airways.
we need to better understand the mechanisms of airway inflammation and airway hyperreactivity, which are two of the main features of asthma.
